lesson.title: Project clinic: ablations, counterexamples and negative results
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: An ablation asks why the system works. A counterexample shows where the explanation stops working.
goals: Design ablations that isolate mechanisms without quietly changing the task.
Interpret interacting components using a small factorial experiment.
Turn failures and negative results into bounded, useful conclusions.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
A new system adds caching and batching and finishes in 40 ms instead of 100 ms. Which change helped? The final comparison cannot tell us. We will switch each mechanism on and off, then test the assumptions behind the explanation.

Bring the question and baseline from lessons 32–33. The four-cell numbers are original hypothetical measurements for reasoning, not an actual benchmark. This supplemental clinic is not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment; assessment rules, required deliverables and deadlines remain unverified.

sections.title: From a system result to a mechanism claim
sections.html:
If a system changes batching, caching and candidate selection together, its final win leaves three possible causes and their interactions. To isolate one, remove or vary it while keeping the same task, quality requirement and timing protocol. This is why an ablation is more informative than another final-system chart.

But removal must leave a coherent system. A cache removal that leaves invalid pointers does not measure caching's value. A fixed-parameter ablation asks about a local effect at one configuration. A retuned ablation asks how well the system can do without that component. They are different questions; report both when relevant and label them.

Pick controls from the explanation. If benefits supposedly come from smarter candidates, match candidate counts. If from better memory use, match memory. For learning, consider a simple model, equal training budgets or random-label control. An obviously broken or unfairly tuned comparison cannot establish necessity.

Key takeaway

“Without X” is meaningful only when the remaining system still implements a coherent comparison.

sections.title: Worked example: interactions between cache and batching
sections.html:
Use the same workload and quality in all four cells. With cache off and batching off, latency t00=100 ms. Batching alone gives t01=80 ms. Cache alone gives t10=70 ms. Both give t11=40 ms.

First hold batching off: cache saves 100−70=30 ms. With batching on, cache saves 80−40=40 ms. Next hold cache off: batching saves 100−80=20 ms. With cache on, batching saves 70−40=30 ms. The effect depends on the other component.

If savings were additive, both would take 100−30−20=50 ms. The hypothetical result is 40 ms, an extra 10 ms saving. Define signed latency interaction I=t11−t10−t01+t00=40−70−80+100=−10 ms. Negative here means latency below the additive prediction. Repeat the four cells and inspect variability before trusting this effect.

A helps only when B is present. Is A useless?

No. The evidence suggests an interaction. Trace cache hits, requests and scheduling to test a cause; arithmetic alone does not prove it. Also state the metric scale: additive milliseconds and multiplicative speedup are different analyses.

sections.title: Stress the assumptions deliberately
sections.html:
Write an assumption ledger with five columns: assumption, reason needed, deliberate violation, predicted failure, observed result. That turns a vague “robustness test” into a checkable question.

For a learned estimator, hold out a template or change the data distribution. For ANN, try a selective filter, near-tied neighbors, skewed clusters, deletes or an embedding-version change. For document processing, use a long document, OCR noise, ambiguity, conflicting evidence or a model revision. For disaggregation, try cold caches, hot-page contention, network delay, partial failures and ownership churn.

Choose cases relevant to the intended claim. Start with a small reproducible counterexample where the state can be inspected. The goal is to discover a boundary, not to manufacture an irrelevant corner case against another method. Keep input, expected behavior, actual trace and explanation together.

sections.title: A negative result is a result after the controls are checked
sections.html:
Suppose adaptive ANN search performs 30% fewer distance calculations but user latency does not change. First verify result quality, implementation, baseline resources, workload generator and timing boundary. Then inspect where time went rather than immediately adding another model.

An original breakdown might show host orchestration and transfer dominate. Reduced device work can be real without improving that host-bound regime. The next experiment could increase batch size or remove transfers under an explicitly different boundary. Preserve the original negative result; do not rewrite it as a success.

Q-error improves but runtime worsens. Is the study invalid?

Not automatically. After correctness and timing checks, test whether inference overhead, plan-threshold errors or metric misalignment explains it. A controlled mismatch is useful evidence. Record exploratory datasets instead of searching until a favorable one appears and presenting only that run; freeze a confirmatory protocol for a stronger claim.

sections.title: Revise the claim and consultation decisions
sections.html:
Sort planned claims into supported, not established and contradicted using the actual evidence. If batching helps only at high arrival rates, replace a universal speed claim with that measured range. Add the counterexample and state which assumption changes there.

Bring the four-cell comparison, one failure trace, assumption ledger and proposed scope change to consultation. A decision record can contain date, evidence, decision, rationale, owner and next check; it is a suggested working aid, not an official submission form.

The gain appears only after removing high-contention runs. What should the report say?

Show all runs and the contention-dependent breakdown. Restrict the benefit to the measured low-contention regime. If high contention belongs to the target workload, include its failure in the overall conclusion. Removing a run solely because it hurts the headline is not a valid exclusion.

Key takeaway

A credible limitation explains when and why the result changes.

quiz.question: What does a four-cell experiment with A off/on and B off/on reveal that two independent ablations may miss?
options: The official grading rubric.
A guarantee of generalization to every workload.
Interactions between A and B.
Whether all bugs are gone.
quiz.explanation: Compute each effect with the other component fixed. In the lesson cache saves 30 ms without batching and 40 ms with batching; batching saves 20 or 30 ms. The signed latency interaction is 40−70−80+100=−10 ms, an extra saving beyond the additive prediction, subject to repeated-measurement uncertainty.

questions.question: Why might a retuned ablation be useful in addition to a fixed-parameter ablation?
options: It eliminates the need for a baseline.
Retuning always proves the new component is necessary.
It permits tuning on final test answers.
Removing a component may change the appropriate settings for the remaining system.
questions.explanation: The two designs answer different questions: the component’s local effect versus the best achievable system without it.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: If only low-contention workloads improve, what should the claim say?
options: The system is always faster.
The system improves in the measured low-contention regime and has a stated high-contention limitation.
The negative cases cannot be real.
High-contention runs should be hidden.
questions.explanation: A bounded operating range is defensible. A general claim that omits relevant failures is not.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Distance evaluations drop 30%, but latency is unchanged. What is a plausible next step?
options: Assume the timer is wrong without checking.
Stop reporting latency.
Measure a time breakdown to see whether transfers or orchestration dominate.
Invent a latency improvement from the arithmetic reduction.
questions.explanation: Reduced internal work need not reduce end-to-end time. A breakdown tests the bottleneck explanation.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What makes a negative result useful?
options: Hiding unfavorable tests.
Changing metrics until one improves.
A claim that research requires positive speedup.
A meaningful hypothesis, validated implementation/protocol, and an explained operating boundary.
questions.explanation: Careful negative evidence can falsify an assumption and guide the next experiment.

lqo.title: Is Your Learned Query Optimizer Behaving As You Expect? A Machine Learning Perspective
lqo.authors: Claude Lehmann, Pavel Sulimov, Kurt Stockinger
lqo.supports: An end-to-end learned-optimizer evaluation framework; sensitivity to training/test design; PostgreSQL wins in most tested comparisons, depending on split. This is evidence about the evaluated systems and protocol, not impossibility of learned optimization.

grasp.authors: Peizhi Wu, Rong Kang, Tieying Zhang, Jianjun Chen, Ryan Marcus, Zachary G. Ives
grasp.supports: GRASP learns from queries and observed cardinalities without raw data access; compositional models target incomplete or imbalanced join templates and range-predicate shifts. Evaluated on three database instances.
